hops.title: The polywater scare and a sweaty T-shirt
hops.text: In the 1960s, chemists found a strange liquid inside glass tubes as thin as a hair. It was syrupy, froze at minus 40 degrees Fahrenheit and boiled near 400. Some feared this "polywater" might spread and change ordinary water. Then Bell Labs physicist Denis Rousseau played a hard game of handball, wrung sweat from his T-shirt and tested its chemical fingerprint. It closely matched polywater. Polywater turned out to be ordinary water loaded with impurities, and sweat was one clue to where they came from.

sources.citation: Ramirez A. The Rise and Fall of Polywater. Distillations, Science History Institute (2020).
Rousseau DL. "Polywater" and sweat: similarities between the infrared spectra. Science 171(3967):170-172 (1971); Ramirez A, Science History Institute (2020).

image.caption: The famous "new water" was ordinary water loaded with impurities, and a sweaty shirt helped show it.

hops.title: Why water is a weak fix for a spicy chili
hops.text: When a chili pepper sets your mouth on fire, the usual move is to gulp water. It helps, but less than milk does. Capsaicin, the chemical behind the burn, is mostly water-repelling, so it dissolves poorly in water. Penn State researchers gave 72 volunteers spicy tomato juice, then tested seven drinks, water included. Chilled whole milk and chilled skim milk both eased the burn more than room-temperature water did. That hints that something in milk, perhaps its protein, may grab capsaicin; the study did not test this.

sources.citation: Nolden AA, Lenart G, Hayes JE. Putting out the fire - Efficacy of common beverages in reducing oral burn from capsaicin. Physiology & Behavior 208:112557 (2019).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A teenager fanning their mouth at a kitchen table with a red chili pepper, a glass of water and a half-empty glass of milk.
image.caption: Capsaicin dissolves poorly in water. In the study, chilled milk eased the burn more than room-temperature water.

hops.afterHeading: Explain: why the Bay barely warmed
hops.title: Water-cooled underwear inside a spacesuit
hops.text: Spacewalkers face temperatures up to 250 degrees Fahrenheit in direct sunlight, and their own body heat builds up inside the sealed suit. So the first thing an astronaut pulls on is stretchy spandex long underwear threaded with about 300 feet of thin tubes. A pump and chiller in the backpack send cold water through the tubes, right next to the skin. Water suits the job because of its high specific heat: each gram soaks up a lot of body heat while warming only a little, then carries it away.

sources.citation: NASA Johnson Space Center. Spacewalk Spacesuit Basics (2019).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A stretchy white spacesuit undergarment threaded with loops of thin blue water-filled tubing next to a spacesuit helmet.
image.caption: Water's high specific heat lets chilled water in thin tubes carry a spacewalker's body heat away.
